shorts.title: The Army Built a 572-Foot Train With No Tracks
shorts.hook: In the Arizona desert, the United States Army once tested a vehicle that looked less like a truck...
shorts.narration_text: In the Arizona desert, the United States Army once tested a vehicle that looked less like a truck, and more like an entire transportation system moving under its own power. It was 572 feet long, 13 units in all, a towering control car followed by cargo and power sections. 54 wheels could drive the machine forward. It carried a crew of six, and could haul roughly 150 tons of cargo. And despite being called an overland train, it needed no railroad, no rails, no prepared highway. It was designed to keep moving when conventional transportation infrastructure simply ended. This was the LeTourneau TC 497 Overland Train Mark II.

shorts.title: Why the TC-497 Put Electric Motors in Its Wheels
shorts.hook: A trailer no longer had to be nothing more than dead weight behind one tractor.
shorts.narration_text: A trailer no longer had to be nothing more than dead weight behind one tractor. Additional sections could contribute traction of their own. Another section could be added, then another. And power could be distributed through the train instead of asking one tractor at the front to drag everything behind it. LeTourneau had been developing electric wheel technology long before the TC497. Patents filed in the early 1950s described vehicle wheels incorporating electric traction motors directly into the wheel assembly. The basic idea was simple enough to explain in a diagram. Its consequences were enormous. The TC497 was not the first land train. It was the result of years of increasingly ambitious experiments.

shorts.title: 400 Miles With No Road—But How Do You Turn 572 Feet?
shorts.hook: LeTourneau had effectively turned something resembling a convoy into one connected machine.
shorts.narration_text: The LeTourneau had effectively turned something resembling a convoy into one connected machine. Army historical accounts place its maximum speed at roughly 20 miles per hour, and its operating range at around 400 miles. Those figures would be unimpressive for an ordinary highway truck. But the TC497 was not built for an ordinary highway. Its entire purpose was to go where the highway did not exist. But building a machine this long created a problem that had nothing to do with horsepower. How do you make it turn?

shorts.title: The Army Considered a Nuclear Overland Train
shorts.hook: The Army briefly considered taking the concept much further.
shorts.narration_text: And while the conventional TC497 was already an extraordinary machine, the Army briefly considered taking the concept much further. In 1961, an Army research publication discussed using a compact nuclear power plant as a possible source of energy for an overland train. The idea followed naturally from the vehicle's electrical architecture. If the wheels were driven electrically, then the traction system did not fundamentally require a conventional mechanical connection between the power plant and the wheels. Electricity generated by another source could, at least in principle, feed the same kind of distributed drive system.

shorts.title: The Helicopter That Made the 572-Foot Train Obsolete
shorts.hook: A ground vehicle still had to negotiate the terrain in front of it.
shorts.narration_text: A ground vehicle still had to negotiate the terrain in front of it. Rivers mattered. Steep ridges mattered. Soft ground mattered. Large dunes mattered. A heavy-lift helicopter could bypass many of those terrain obstacles entirely. Aircrafts such as Sikorsky's S -64 Sky Crane and the Army's CH -54 Tarhe represented a fundamentally different solution to the logistics problem. Instead of carrying a supply system slowly across difficult terrain, vertical lift could move heavy loads directly between points without following the landscape between them. Army historical accounts are unusually clear about what happened next. Heavy -lift helicopter technology made the Overland train increasingly obsolete before the concept could become an operational fleet.
